text: Six months ago I signed up for my first half marathon, mostly because a friend dared me. Today I finished my longest training run so far, eighteen kilometers, and I want to write down what actually helped, because I wish somebody had told me this in the beginning. One, slow down. Seriously. Most of my runs are at a pace where I can still talk, and that felt embarrassing at first. It is also the reason my knees still work. Two, plan your week like a meeting you cannot cancel. Mine is three easy runs, one interval session, one long run on Sunday, and two real rest days. Rest is part of training, not a reward for it. Three, eat before you think you need to. I learned the hard way that a banana at kilometer twelve is too late. Four, find your people. I joined a small running group that meets on Tuesday evenings at the river, and the difference is huge. On days when I would have skipped, somebody sends a message saying see you at seven. Five, track how you feel, not only how fast you are. I keep a tiny notebook with three words per run, like tired, windy, proud. When I read it back, the bad days barely matter anymore. The biggest surprise was how much running changed my head. I sleep better, I handle stressful meetings better, and I stopped checking my phone first thing in the morning. Some mornings the only goal is to get out of the door, and that is enough. If you are on the fence about starting, this is your sign. Begin with ten minutes, walk whenever you want, and do not compare your first week with somebody else's tenth year. Race day is in six weeks, and I will keep you posted. Tell me your favorite running route in the comments, I need new ideas. 🏃 #running #halfmarathon #marathontraining #runnersofinstagram #beginnerrunner

text: One year ago I cleared out my wardrobe and kept only 35 pieces. Here is what I learned, because a lot of you asked about it. I was not trying to become a minimalist. I was tired of standing in front of a full closet every morning with nothing to wear. So I tried a simple experiment. I took everything out, put it on the bed, and sorted it into three piles: love, maybe, and never wear. The never pile was shockingly big, almost half. Some pieces still had tags. That was an uncomfortable moment, but also a useful one. The first rule I set is a color palette. Mine is beige, white, navy, olive, and black, with one accent color per season. When everything matches, you can combine any top with any bottom, and getting dressed takes two minutes. The second rule is fit over trends. I bought fewer trendy items and invested in a good pair of jeans, a wool coat, a pair of leather boots, and three well-cut shirts. I look for natural fabrics like cotton, wool, and linen, which last longer and feel better. The third rule is the one in, one out policy. If I buy something new, one piece leaves the closet. I sell it, donate it, or hand it down to a friend. Fourth, I buy second-hand whenever I can. Around sixty percent of my wardrobe now comes from thrift shops and online resale, and I have never felt less stylish. If anything, my outfits are more personal than before. The biggest change is not visual, it is emotional. I spend less money, I make faster decisions, and I feel more like myself. Some weeks I repeat outfits and nobody notices, which is a relief. If you want to try this, start small. Pick one shelf or one drawer, and ask of each item whether you would buy it again today. text: Some paintings fight me from the first brushstroke. This one started as a quick blue sketch and slowly turned into a warm evening scene I had not planned at all. I work in thin layers and wait for each one to dry before deciding what comes next. Some days I add a single line and leave the studio. Other days I paint for ten hours and forget to eat. text: A lot of you asked me when a painting is finished, and honestly, I am never completely sure. For me it is finished when I stop wanting to change it, and that moment can take weeks. This piece is part of a new series about memory and light, which I will show in a small group exhibition next spring. Let me walk you through how it came to be. It began with an old photograph of my grandmother's kitchen, the one with yellow curtains and a window that always had too much sun. I did not want to copy the photo. I wanted to paint what it felt like to stand in that room as a child. So I started with a rough orange ground and added thin layers of blue and green on top. Each layer changed the mood completely. Around the sixth layer I almost threw the canvas away, because it looked muddy and tired. I put it facing the wall for two weeks. When I turned it around again I saw immediately what it needed, a single bright vertical shape where the window would be. It took me five minutes. The previous five weeks were the real work. I share this because I think social media often makes art look fast and certain. In my studio it is slow and full of doubt, and I have learned to trust that doubt as part of the process. Some practical things people asked about: I use professional acrylics on cotton canvas, a mix of brushes and a palette knife, and I varnish everything at the end. I am also preparing a small edition of prints, so more people can own something original at a fair price. If you would like to be notified, the link is in my bio. Thank you for following the process, and tell me about a piece of art that stayed in your memory. 🎨 #art #contemporaryart #acrylicpainting #studiolife #artistsoninstagram

text: Sunday is slow cooking day at our place, and today I finally wrote down my tomato sauce, which friends keep asking for. It takes three hours, but only fifteen minutes of that is real work. Start with two tablespoons of olive oil in a heavy pot. Add one finely chopped onion, one carrot, and one celery stalk, and let them cook gently for ten minutes until soft and sweet. This base is what gives the sauce its depth, so do not rush it. Add three cloves of sliced garlic for the last two minutes. Pour in two cans of whole peeled tomatoes and crush them with your hands. It is messy and it is also the most satisfying part. Add a good pinch of salt, a bay leaf, a splash of red wine if you have some open, and a piece of parmesan rind, which melts into the sauce and adds a savory note. Now comes the important part. Turn the heat to the lowest setting, put the lid slightly ajar, and leave it alone. Stir every thirty minutes or so. Taste at the end and adjust. Sometimes a teaspoon of sugar helps if the tomatoes are sharp. Remove the bay leaf and the rind, add fresh basil, and you are done. A few tips from many failed attempts. Do not use too much garlic or it becomes bitter. Do not skip the salt at the beginning, because it helps the vegetables release their flavor. Always cook a double batch, since the sauce freezes perfectly for three months. Use it for pasta, lasagna, shakshuka, or as a pizza base. My grandmother never measured anything, so my version is an approximation of her taste memory, but every Sunday it brings the whole family to the table. Food is not only about eating, it is about slowing down together. Save this recipe for your next free Sunday and let me know in the comments what you will cook with it. 🍅 #homecooking #pastasauce #sundaycooking #foodie #recipe

text: Two weeks alone in Japan taught me more than I expected, and I want to share the honest version of how it went. I was nervous before leaving, mostly because I do not speak any Japanese and had never traveled alone for more than a weekend. Here is what helped. First, I booked only the first and the last night in advance. Everything in between stayed flexible, and that freedom led to my best days, like a spontaneous detour to a small coastal town where an old woman served me tea and showed me photos of her garden. Second, I bought a rail pass early and used it more than planned. Trains are punctual, clean, and quiet, and watching the landscape change from the window is half the fun. Third, I learned ten simple phrases, such as thank you, excuse me, and where is the station. People appreciate the effort so much, even if you pronounce everything wrong, which I did. Fourth, cash still matters. Many small restaurants and shrines only accept coins and notes, so keep some with you. Fifth, eat where the locals eat. My favorite meals were at tiny counters with only eight seats, where you point at a picture and trust the cook. I never had a bad one. Sixth, respect the quiet. People speak softly on trains and in public places, so keep your phone on silent and your voice low. It makes everything calmer for everybody. There were hard moments too. On day four I got lost in a huge station for almost an hour, felt very small, and wondered why I had come. A stranger noticed, walked me to the correct platform, and refused any thanks. That moment changed my whole trip. If you are thinking about traveling solo, my advice is to start somewhere safe, keep your plan loose, and give yourself permission to rest. Save this post for later and tell me your dream destination below. 🌸 #travel #japan #solotravel #traveldiary #wanderlust

text: First week in my new role and the biggest lesson is already clear. Nobody expects you to know everything on day one, but everybody remembers if you ask good questions. text: I have sat in more than forty job interviews over the last years, on both sides of the table, so here is what I wish every candidate knew. First, preparation is not about memorizing answers. It is about knowing three or four stories from your work that you can adapt to almost any question. Pick moments where you solved a problem, handled a conflict, or learned something from a mistake. Write each one down in simple steps: the situation, what you did, and what happened afterwards. Second, research the company beyond the homepage. Read recent news, look at what their team posts, and find one real challenge they face. Then connect your experience to that challenge. Hiring managers notice immediately when someone has done this work. Third, ask questions that show you want to understand the job, not only get it. For example, what does success look like after six months, or what is the hardest part of this role that nobody mentions in the description. Fourth, practise out loud. Reading your answers in your head feels very different from saying them. Record yourself on your phone or practise with a friend, and trim anything that rambles. Fifth, handle rejection like data. Three years ago I was turned down for the exact role I started this week. I asked for feedback, and the recruiter told me honestly that my project management experience was too thin. I took a course, led two small projects, and applied again when I was ready. The no was not the end of the story, it was a to-do list. Finally, take care of yourself on the day. Sleep, eat something, and arrive early so you are not rushing. You are interviewing them as much as they are interviewing you. If you are job hunting right now, I am rooting for you. Share this with someone who needs it today, and tell me your best interview tip in the comments. 💼 #career #jobsearch #interviewtips #professionalgrowth #worklife

text: Eight months ago I had never opened a computer case. Last weekend I finished my first gaming PC, and I want to share the whole process, including the mistakes, because most guides only show the shiny result. First, the budget. I set a hard limit of 900 euros and stuck a note on my monitor. When you start reading forums, every part suddenly feels necessary, and that note kept me honest. Second, order matters. Pick the processor and the graphics card first, because they decide what everything else has to support. Then choose a motherboard with the matching socket, two sticks of memory so the system can use dual channel, and a power supply with some headroom. A cheap power supply is the one place I would not save money. Third, I used an online compatibility checker, and it caught a mistake before I ordered: my first cooler was too tall for the case. Fourth, the build. I watched two tutorials, laid every part out on a table, and touched the metal case now and then to avoid static. Installing the processor felt scary, but it only fits one way, and a small triangle marks the right corner. The most annoying moment was a missing standoff screw that I found under the sofa an hour later. Fifth, the first boot. Nothing appeared on the screen, my heart dropped, and then I noticed that the monitor cable was plugged into the motherboard instead of the graphics card. Apparently that happens to almost everyone. Sixth, cable management. I spent two hours on it, and nobody will ever see the result except me, but opening the case now feels peaceful. If you are thinking about building your own PC, the community is incredibly kind, and almost every problem has been solved by somebody before you. The best part is not the frame rate. It is understanding what is inside the machine you use every day. Save this post for your own build, and tell me which game you would play first. 🖥️ #pcbuild #gamingpc #pcgaming #techsetup #firstbuild

text: Last night I finally managed to see Saturn's rings through my small backyard telescope, and I am still thinking about it. I want to share how you can do the same, because I always believed this needed expensive equipment and a mountain top. It does not. A basic telescope with a 70 mm lens and a cheap phone adapter is enough. First, pick the right night. Check a cloud forecast and look for a time when the moon is not full, because bright moonlight washes out fainter objects. Second, give your eyes twenty minutes to adapt to the dark. Put your phone on red-light mode and resist the urge to check it. Third, start with the easy targets. The moon is spectacular even for beginners, you can see craters and mountain shadows along the edge of the lit area. Jupiter shows its four big moons as tiny dots in a line, and Galileo discovered them in 1610 with a device much worse than yours. Saturn is the real showstopper. When its rings appear as a small tilted ellipse, you realize that you are looking at light that left the planet more than an hour earlier. Fourth, use a free sky map app to find the planets. I rely on one that works offline, because the best viewing spots often have no signal. Fifth, be patient. The atmosphere makes images wobble, so wait for moments of steady air. And do not expect colorful photos like the ones from space agencies. Those images are long exposures and processed data. What you see with your own eyes is much quieter, but it is real and it is yours. I started this hobby during a difficult winter, and now it is the thing I look forward to every clear evening. If you would like a beginner shopping list or a monthly sky calendar, let me know in the comments. And tell me, what is the first object you would like to see? 🪐 #astronomy #space #stargazing #science #telescope

text: Quick reminder: high blood pressure usually causes no symptoms, so the only way to know is to measure it. text: A year ago I realized that I could not remember the last time I had seen a doctor when nothing was wrong. I was healthy, busy, and a little proud of never being sick. Then a colleague my age was diagnosed with high blood pressure at a routine visit, and she had felt nothing at all. That conversation changed my thinking. Prevention is boring, and that is exactly why it works. Here is what I did, in case it helps you. First, I booked a general check-up. It took ten minutes on the phone and an hour at the practice. They measured my blood pressure, took a blood sample, and asked about my sleep, my stress, and my family history. Everything was fine, but now I have numbers to compare with next year. Second, I checked my vaccination record and found out that my tetanus booster was overdue, because it is recommended roughly every ten years and I had simply forgotten. One quick appointment fixed it. Third, I went to the dentist. I had skipped it for almost three years, and I paid for that with a small filling, which could have been much worse. Fourth, I started moving on purpose. Health organizations recommend around 150 minutes of moderate activity per week, and I reach that by walking to work and taking a long walk on Sundays. No gym, no equipment. Fifth, I made sleep a priority: phone out of the bedroom, the same bedtime on most nights, and no coffee after two. It is not exciting, but I wake up differently. Sixth, I put my next appointments into my calendar, so I do not rely on motivation. I am not a doctor, and this is not medical advice. What I can say is that most prevention is small, scheduled, and easy to postpone, until it is not. If you have been delaying a check-up, consider this your reminder. Call tomorrow morning, before the day gets busy. Share this with someone who always says they are too healthy to go, and tell me what you are going to book. 🩺 #health #prevention #checkup #wellbeing #selfcare

text: Two years ago a handful of neighbors decided to start a monthly dinner for people of different faiths and none. Today more than sixty people come, and I am often asked how we got started, so here is the honest story. It began after a town hall meeting about the future of our community hall. People were passionate, a few were angry, and I noticed that many of us had never spoken to each other outside of such meetings. A Muslim neighbor, a Lutheran pastor, a Jewish teacher, and I sat in a cafe afterwards and decided to try something simple: a shared meal. Step one was the venue. We asked the city office for permission to use the community hall, and the clerk helped us with the forms. It took three weeks and one very friendly phone call. Step two was the ground rules, which we print on every table. We listen first. Nobody tries to convert anybody. We do not discuss party politics, and personal questions are optional. Step three was the food. Everyone brings a dish and a card with the ingredients, so people with halal, kosher, vegetarian, or allergy needs can eat safely. We draw seat numbers from a hat to mix the table. Step four was a quiet room next to the hall, where guests can pray or rest. Not many use it, but those who do are very grateful. What surprised me most is how ordinary the conversations are. People talk about their children, their jobs, their grandmothers' recipes, and sometimes about what a festival means to them. Of course, not everything is easy. We have had awkward silences, a few misunderstandings, and one evening when the soup ran out. But we always come back to the table. If you would like to start something like this where you live, begin small, ask your local council or community center for a room, and invite people through schools, congregations, and clubs. You do not need experts, just curiosity and enough chairs. Share this with a neighbor and tell me what you would put on the table. 🤝 #community #interfaith #neighbors #dialogue
